newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says it will meet EMU deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: France says it will meet EMU deficit goal.

text.p: The French government reaffirmed its determination on Wednesday to hit crucial deficit targets this year to qualify for a single European currency despite a slight overshooting in 1996.
"I confirm that France will keep to its objective of limiting its deficits to three percent of GDP," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters.

Arthuis said he expected the French economy to pick up steam and repeated that he considered the government's official forecast of 2.3 percent gross domestic product growth (GDP) for 1997 to be a floor estimate.
The dollar's recent rally, coupled with an improving economic performance, "puts us in an encouraging context and 2.3 percent growth is a minimum" this year, he said.
Earlier, Arthuis announced France's 1996 public deficits would equal 4.1 percent of GDP, just over its four percent target.
France's 1996 budget deficit will total 295.4 billion francs ($51.9 billion), compared to the government's initial target of 287.8 billion. It is 28 billion francs lower than the 1995 gap.
Arthuis said government spending rose 1.7 percent in 1996, the first time the government has kept spending below inflation. Prices rose about two percent in 1996, he said.
The central government budget deficit represents some 3.7 percent of GDP and Arthuis said the 4.1 percent figure included other items such as the shortfall in the social security system.
Confirming French newspaper reports, Arthuis said that as in past years, the government was prepared to freeze spending lines to keep its deficits to three percent of GDP.

It cancelled about 31 billion francs in spending in 1996 to narrow the deficit. This year -- a crucial year for countries trying to meet the norms for monetary union -- it has resorted to measures such as using a 37.5 billion franc transfer from state-owned France Telecom to cut the annual deficit.
Arthuis said he was pleased by the final budgetary result.
"It's good news given the economy was not robust in 1996. Despite this, we were able to arrive at a deficit of 295.4 billion francs by controlling our public spending," he said.
The initial 1996 budget law was based on a growth forecast of 2.8 percent, far above the final result of 1.3 percent.
Arthuis said the deficit overshoot did not worry him. "It is a slippage of 0.1 percentage point," he said.

The Maastrict treaty on monetary union - which sets goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation and public budgets -- calls for European nations to have deficits of no more than three percent of GDP in 1997 to qualify for the single currency.
It is due to go into effect on January 1, 1999.

At the news conference, Arthuis said he was satisfied with the dollar's recent rise against major currencies and added that he hoped the new foreign exchange parities would be maintained. It was trading close to 5.70 francs on Wednesday, compared with about five francs late last year.
He said the stronger dollar was good for French growth and said stability at these levels would be positive.
"I am satisfied...we must consolidate current foreign exchange parities," he said.
"Economic growth needs stable and equitable parities."
